newsitem.title: CHINA: NYSE says to list at least 75 non-U.S. firms in 97.
newsitem.headline: NYSE says to list at least 75 non-U.S. firms in 97.

text.p: The New York Stock Exchange expects to list at least a record 75 companies from outside the United States this year, compared with 59 in 1996, NYSE senior vice president James Cochrane said on Friday.

"I use the number 75, but frankly I'll probably be a little disappointed if that's what we do," Cochrane told reporters at a seminar in Shanghai on China's accounting standards. "I think we can do a bit better."
The NYSE had 290 non-U.S. companies with common stock listed on the exchange at the end of 1996.
But Cochrane said it was difficult to forecast exact numbers because the listings would depend on the health of the securities markets in the local country and its politics.
"Numerically, when the year is over, I suspect that South America and Europe will be our biggest source of non-U.S. companies," he said, adding that Brazil was one of the brighter prospects.
"This region (Asia) looks exciting but it varies on a country-by-country basis," Cochrane said.
The exchange expected to list two or three companies from Japan this summer and had "several opportunities" in South Korea, he said, but declined to name specific companies.

There were also a number of Chinese companies in the pipeline, Cochrane said. China has two companies with shares listed in New York and five more with listings both in New York and Hong Kong, according to Chinese officials.

"In Southeast Asia, our most exciting short- and medium-term prospect is Indonesia, in terms of dollar amounts of the offerings, size of the companies and the probable appetite for the securities in the United States," Cochrane said.
He added one or two companies each from Singapore, the Philipines and Thailand were expected to list this year.
"We'll do a couple more from Australia, but the big one will be Telstra -- that's a significant flotation," he said.

The government-owned Telstra Corp, one of Australia's main telecommunications companies, is planning a public offering of shares comprising a one-third stake in the company worth a total of at least A$8 billion, according to analysts.
"How much of Telstra will be sold in the North America market no one knows, I think that's still being discussed," Cochrane said.
"While it's not fixed, perhaps a third might be coming our way," he said.
